content.text: You’ve seen how you can type values for strings directly into your code, but Swift also has a feature called string interpolation – the ability to place variables inside your strings to make them more useful.
You can place any type of variable inside your string – all you have to do is write a backslash, `\`, followed by your variable name in parentheses. For example:

content.code:
var score = 85
var str = "Your score was \(score)"

content.text: As you can see in the playground output, that sets the `str` variable to be “Your score was 85”.
You can do this as many times as you need, making strings out of strings if you want:

content.code: var results = "The test results are here: \(str)"

content.text: As you’ll see later on, string interpolation isn’t just limited to placing variables – you can actually run code inside there.
